title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: The Parallel-Trends Assumption: The Essential Test
text:
The Parallel-Trends Assumption: The Essential Test
DiD compares the change in an intervention population with the change in a comparison population. Its central identifying assumption is that, without the intervention, their outcome trends would have been parallel (or sufficiently comparable after appropriate adjustment). Similar baseline admission rates do not establish parallel trends. Inspect several pre-intervention periods and consider differences in population need, coding, service capacity, concurrent initiatives and spillovers.
For a numerical example, suppose emergency admission rates per 1,000 eligible person-years are:



Locality

The illustrative DiD estimate is −15 admissions per 1,000 eligible person-years: (100 − 120) − (105 − 110) = −15. This is a relative change, not automatically 15 admissions prevented by the pathway. A causal interpretation requires a defensible design and assumptions, appropriate uncertainty estimates and no material interference or anticipatory changes. If the two populations have changing age, deprivation or frailty profiles, consider how rates and adjustment should reflect those changes.
When services roll out at different times, a conventional two-way fixed-effects DiD can be misleading if effects differ across groups or over time. Use methods appropriate to staggered adoption and examine event-time patterns rather than assuming a standard DiD model is valid.

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Why DiD Matters for Healthcare Decision-Making
text:
Why DiD Matters for Healthcare Decision-Making
Healthcare systems frequently implement interventions:

gradually
in some places before others
under different operational conditions

This makes DiD especially useful when:

RCTs are unrealistic
phased roll-out exists
comparator organisations or places are available

Without comparators:
decision-makers risk attributing:

system-wide improvement

to

local intervention impact

A useful question becomes:

Would similar improvement have happened elsewhere anyway?

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

Key Message
Good evaluation becomes stronger when healthcare systems ask:

Did trajectories change?

and

Compared with what?

rather than simply asking:

Did outcomes improve?

Pragmatic evaluation methods such as:

Interrupted Time Series (ITS)

and

Difference-in-Differences (DiD)

help strengthen confidence when Randomised Controlled Trials are not practical.

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:
Part 3 Reflection
Before acting on evaluation findings, ask:

Could this improvement reflect an existing trend — or would similar change have happened elsewhere anyway?

Good evaluation moves beyond:

Did outcomes improve?

to ask:

How confident are we that the intervention genuinely contributed to change?
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:
An Evaluation Design Checklist
Before selecting a statistical technique, record:

Decision and estimand: What commissioning decision is at stake, and whose outcome under what intervention versus what alternative are we trying to estimate?
Population and eligibility: Who was eligible, including those who did not take up the offer? Are cohorts fixed at baseline or updated over time?
Intervention and timing: What changed, when, for whom and with what implementation intensity? Was introduction gradual?
Outcome and follow-up: Are the outcomes meaningful, measured consistently and assessed over a suitable horizon? Include safety and unintended consequences.
Comparison and assumptions: Is a counterfactual plausible? What selection, confounding, spillover or simultaneous changes threaten it?
Data and precision: Are denominators, missingness, seasonality, clustering and statistical uncertainty adequately addressed?
Equity and complexity: Could results vary by frailty, age, deprivation or place? How will changing need, mortality and competing events be considered?
Triangulation and use: What do patients, carers and staff say? What implementation and economic evidence is needed? What decision would different findings support?
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:
Different Questions Require Different Evidence
Causal impact evaluation asks whether an intervention made a difference compared with an alternative. Process evaluation asks whether it was delivered as intended. Theory-based or realist evaluation examines how, why and under what circumstances outcomes may arise. Equity analysis asks who benefits or is missed. Economic evaluation asks whether benefits justify resources and opportunity costs.
These approaches complement rather than substitute for one another. Interviews and implementation evidence can strengthen an explanation, but do not by themselves establish the number of admissions prevented. Conversely, a credible average impact estimate does not reveal why the pathway worked, whether patients experienced better care or whether it was worth the investment.
For an integrated frailty portfolio, start by assessing impact at the eligible cohort/model-of-care level, where the causal design permits. Pathway analysis may explain mechanisms and variation, but comparing patients who received different components rarely isolates each component’s causal effect because clinical need influences exposure. Module 17 develops this issue in detail.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Sensitivity Analysis: Would the Conclusion Survive Reasonable Alternatives?
text:
Sensitivity Analysis: Would the Conclusion Survive Reasonable Alternatives?
A single result should not be presented as certain. Test how findings change when plausible assumptions vary—for example, different start dates, pre-intervention periods, comparison localities, eligible cohorts, seasonal specifications or adjustment for changing population need. Report the range of credible estimates, not only the most favourable one. These checks do not rescue a fundamentally invalid design, and scenario ranges are not the same as statistical confidence intervals.

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Seven Steps for a Proportionate NHS Evaluation
text:
Seven Steps for a Proportionate NHS Evaluation








Step
What to document
Example: community frailty pathway




1. Commissioning decision
Continue, redesign, expand or stop? By when?
Decide whether to extend the pathway to other PCNs


2. Target effect (estimand)
Eligible population, intervention, comparator, outcome and follow-up
Difference in 12-month emergency admission rate for eligible older adults if offered the pathway versus usual care


3. Theory of change
What should change first, and why?
Earlier assessment → quicker community response → fewer avoidable crises


4. Data and feasibility
Eligibility, dates, exposure, outcomes, denominators, missingness, linkage and approvals
Monthly admission data, GP population registers and service referral logs


5. Design and threats
Comparison strategy, assumptions, competing changes, contamination
Controlled ITS; check whether comparator PCNs received similar services


6. Analysis plan
Primary outcome, subgroups, uncertainty, sensitivity analyses and stopping rules
Pre-specify 12-month rate and adjustment for seasonality


7. Reporting and use
Limitations, implementation, patient experience, equity, costs and decision thresholds
Report both impact estimate and whether the pathway reached those in greatest need









TipThe estimand: specify what “impact” means



“Did the pathway work?” is too vague for analysis. An estimand is the precise effect the evaluation seeks to estimate: for which population, under which intervention compared with which alternative, over what period, on which outcome?
For example, the effect of offering the pathway to everyone eligible differs from the effect among people who actually received intensive MDT support. These are different questions and may require different designs.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Define the Population, Denominator and Outcome Fairly
text:
Define the Population, Denominator and Outcome Fairly
Raw activity counts can fall because the population at risk shrank, fewer people were eligible, patients died or records became incomplete. Where appropriate, compare rates using a clearly defined denominator or person-time rather than counts alone.








Measure
Potential problem
Better question




Total admissions
Changing population size or case mix
Admissions per 1,000 eligible people or person-years, with suitable adjustment


Admissions among pathway users
People selected because they recently had a crisis
What happened to all eligible people, including those not referred?


Average admissions per patient
Follow-up differs because people enter at different dates
How much person-time was each patient observed for?


Admission rate among survivors
Death removes high-risk people from observation
Were mortality and competing events considered alongside admissions?


Crude comparison between localities
Age, deprivation and frailty profiles differ
How would findings change after appropriate standardisation or adjustment?



For frailty and end-of-life pathways, interpret activity together with need, complexity, mortality, safety and patient goals. A lower admission rate is not automatically a better outcome. Avoid conditioning the primary analysis only on surviving patients when survival may itself be affected by the intervention.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Using a Causal Diagram (DAG) to Think Before Adjusting
text:
Using a Causal Diagram (DAG) to Think Before Adjusting
A Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a simple map of hypothesised cause-and-effect relationships. It can help analysts identify variables that might confound an exposure–outcome relationship, and variables that should not automatically be adjusted for.
Baseline frailty / illness severity ──→ MDT referral
             │                            │
             └────────────────────────────→ Emergency admission
                                          ↑
                                  Potential MDT effect
Here baseline severity influences both referral and admissions. A fair comparison may need to account for it. But a measure changed by the MDT—such as improved medication management—may be part of the pathway’s effect; adjusting for it could remove some of the effect being studied. Variables affected by both exposure and outcome-related factors can also introduce collider bias when conditioned on. DAGs clarify assumptions; they do not prove those assumptions are true.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Adjustment, Matching and Weighting: What They Can and Cannot Do
text:
Adjustment, Matching and Weighting: What They Can and Cannot Do








Approach
Basic idea
Important limitation




Regression adjustment
Compare outcomes while accounting for measured baseline differences
Cannot remove bias from unmeasured or badly measured confounders


Propensity-score matching
Match exposed and unexposed people with similar estimated probability of exposure
May discard patients and cannot correct unmeasured confounding


Propensity-score weighting
Reweight groups to improve balance on measured baseline characteristics
Extreme weights and lack of overlap can make estimates unstable


Stratification or standardisation
Compare within need/age strata or apply a common population distribution
Requires adequate information and comparable strata



Practical checks: Are relevant variables measured before treatment? Do intervention and comparison groups overlap in characteristics (positivity)? Are important baseline differences balanced after matching or weighting? Are results robust to alternative adjustment choices? Never present statistical adjustment alone as proof of causality.

When exposure and confounding change over time
In a longer pathway, clinical deterioration may lead to additional support; that support may then alter later deterioration and admission risk. Ordinary regression adjustment for these time-varying factors can introduce bias. Methods such as marginal structural models with inverse-probability weighting or other longitudinal causal approaches may be appropriate, but require specialist design, reliable longitudinal data and strong assumptions. This is a sign to involve experienced evaluators rather than simply adding more variables to a model.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: A Common Retrospective Trap: Immortal Time Bias
text:
A Common Retrospective Trap: Immortal Time Bias
Imagine defining the intervention group as patients who received an MDT review within 90 days, while counting outcomes from the initial eligibility date. To qualify as “reviewed”, patients must remain eligible and observable until their review; those admitted or dying before review may be disproportionately assigned elsewhere or excluded. This can make the intervention appear protective even when it is not.
Avoid this by defining a common time zero (the date eligibility and follow-up begin), aligning eligibility and treatment strategies, and handling treatment initiation over time appropriately. In some settings a target trial emulation framework—explicitly specifying the trial we would ideally run—helps prevent these errors. Merely adjusting for age or frailty will not fix incorrect time alignment.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:
What Is Missing—and Why?

Missing completely at random (MCAR): missingness is unrelated to measured or unmeasured values; uncommon in operational data.
Missing at random (MAR): after conditioning on observed information, missingness does not depend on the missing value itself. Methods such as multiple imputation may be reasonable if assumptions are credible.
Missing not at random (MNAR): missingness still depends on unseen values or other unobserved factors. Sensitivity analysis is particularly important.

For example, frailer patients may be less likely to complete experience questionnaires. Analysing only respondents could overstate satisfaction. Report the amount, pattern and likely causes of missing data; compare characteristics of people with and without records; and test plausible alternative assumptions. Do not automatically replace missing values with zero.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:
Linkage and Measurement Quality
Before analysis, check whether NHS numbers or other permitted identifiers link reliably, whether patient residence and service boundaries changed, whether coding definitions stayed stable, and whether data flows were disrupted. Use appropriate information governance, secure processing and data minimisation. Poor linkage may disproportionately omit people who move, receive care across boundaries or use multiple services.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Patients, PCNs and Months Are Not Independent
text:
Patients, PCNs and Months Are Not Independent
A patient may have repeated attendances; patients within a PCN share staff and pathways; monthly outcomes may be correlated with adjacent months. Standard errors that assume every observation is independent may be too small. Depending on the design, consider cluster-robust uncertainty estimates, mixed-effects models, generalised estimating equations or time-series models that address autocorrelation. With only a few clusters, ordinary cluster-robust methods may be unreliable; seek specialist advice.
The effective amount of information depends on the number of independent units, not just the total number of records. Ten thousand admissions from two PCNs do not provide the same comparative evidence as data from many independently allocated PCNs.
crumbs: 13  Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
section: Matching the Evaluation Method to the Question
text:
Matching the Evaluation Method to the Question
One of the most important principles in evaluation is that the evaluation question should determine the evaluation method.
There is rarely a single “best” evaluation method.
Instead, different methods answer different questions.
Underlying them all is one fundamental idea:

What would probably have happened if the intervention had not taken place?

This is known as the counterfactual.
Different evaluation methods estimate the counterfactual in different ways.








Evaluation Question
What evidence is needed?
Methods Commonly Used




Did it work?
Compare outcomes with what would probably have happened without the intervention.
Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT), Interrupted Time Series (ITS), Difference-in-Differences (DiD), Controlled ITS


How was it implemented?
Examine reach, fidelity, adaptations, resources and experience.
Process evaluation, implementation evaluation, qualitative interviews


Why did it work (or not)?
Explore mechanisms, contexts and alternative explanations.
Qualitative research, Realist Evaluation


Did it work consistently across organisations?
Compare patterns of change across multiple organisations while accounting for differences in starting position, trends and implementation.
Multi-site evaluation, mixed-effects models, meta-analysis


Was it worth it?
Assess incremental outcomes, costs and opportunity costs, using causal estimates where possible.
Health economics, Cost-effectiveness analysis, cost-benefit analysis, cost-utility analysis


Should we scale it?
Integrate impact, implementation, equity, costs and transferability.
Mixed-method evaluation, evidence synthesis, implementation evaluation









TipKey Principle



Good evaluation starts with a clear evaluation question, not a preferred method.
Strong evaluations often combine quantitative and qualitative approaches to understand:

whether an intervention worked
how it was implemented
why it worked (or did not work)
whether it represented good value for money
whether it should be adopted more widely

Impact designs attempt to identify a counterfactual; process, realist and qualitative methods instead investigate implementation, experience and mechanisms. They answer complementary questions and should not all be presented as methods of estimating a counterfactual.
The credibility of a causal conclusion depends on whether the design and its assumptions fit the question and setting—not simply on the sophistication of the statistical model. No evaluation eliminates uncertainty completely.

title: Module 9 — Evaluation Methods in Practice
text:

improvement alone does not prove impact
fair comparison matters
small numbers can mislead
some improvement may happen naturally
trajectories matter
comparison groups strengthen confidence
the evaluation question should determine the evaluation method
ITS and DiD depend on explicit assumptions, not just visible improvements

when no credible counterfactual exists, implementation and contribution evidence can still inform decisions
impact, mechanisms, equity and value are different but complementary questions
a pre-specified evaluation protocol clarifies the estimand, data, design and intended decision
confounding, time alignment, missing data and clustering can undermine apparently convincing results
robustness checks help reveal when conclusions depend on fragile assumptions

Good evaluation asks:

How confident are we that the intervention genuinely contributed to change?

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module you should be able to:
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Understand the difference between risk, probability and certainty.
Recognise common sources of uncertainty in healthcare data and analysis.
Interpret risk estimates appropriately.
Understand why decision-making often occurs despite uncertainty.
Apply a pragmatic approach to making decisions when evidence is incomplete.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Why This Matters
Healthcare leaders are rarely asked to make decisions with complete certainty.
Whether considering a new service model, investing in prevention, redesigning a pathway or implementing a digital solution, there will almost always be uncertainty about future outcomes.
The role of analytics is not to eliminate uncertainty.
The role of analytics is to help decision-makers understand uncertainty well enough to make better decisions.
Good decision-makers do not wait for certainty.
They make informed choices whilst understanding the risks.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Risk Is Not Certainty
A common misunderstanding is to interpret risk estimates as predictions.
Risk describes the likelihood that something may happen.
It does not tell us what will happen for a specific patient, service or population.
For example:



Risk Estimate
Interpretation




80% risk of admission
More likely to occur than not


50% risk of admission
Outcome remains highly uncertain


20% risk of admission
Less likely, but still possible



An 80% risk does not guarantee admission.
A 20% risk does not guarantee safety.
Risk describes probability, not destiny.






Note



A useful question is:
“How often would we expect this outcome to occur in a large group of similar people?”
rather than
“Will this individual definitely experience the outcome?”
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Sources of Uncertainty
Uncertainty exists in all healthcare analyses.
Common sources include:

Random variation.
Incomplete or missing data.
Small sample sizes.
Changes in clinical practice.
Policy changes.
Workforce changes.
Behavioural responses to interventions.
Unexpected external events.

The future rarely behaves exactly like the past.
This means forecasts should always be viewed as estimates rather than promises.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Confidence Intervals
Analysts often report estimates together with a 95% confidence interval.
Rather than providing a single value, confidence intervals recognise that every estimate contains some uncertainty.
For example:



Estimated Readmission Rate
95% Confidence Interval




8.0%
6.9% – 9.1%



6.9% ─────●───── 9.1%
          8%
The confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the true underlying estimate.
Narrow confidence intervals indicate greater precision.
Wider confidence intervals indicate greater uncertainty.
For decision-makers, the important message is often not the exact estimate, but how certain we are about that estimate.






Note



A useful question is:
“How much uncertainty surrounds this estimate?”
rather than
“What is the exact number?”
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Error Bars
Many dashboards and reports include charts with small lines extending above and below a point or bar.
These are known as error bars.
Error bars provide a visual indication of uncertainty around an estimate.
Larger error bars suggest greater uncertainty.
Smaller error bars suggest greater precision.
Two organisations may appear to perform differently, but if their error bars overlap substantially, the apparent difference may simply reflect normal variation rather than a meaningful difference.
Error bars therefore encourage caution when comparing organisations or services.
Hospital A

    ●
  ─────

Hospital B

    ●
──────────
They remind us that every estimate contains uncertainty.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Interpreting a P-value
A p-value answers one question: Could this observed difference simply be due to chance?
                    What does a p-value tell us?

            Observed difference between two groups
                           |
                           v
        Could this difference simply be due to chance?
                           |
          +     -+     -+
          |                                 |
     p < 0.05                         p >= 0.05
          |                                 |
          v                                 v
Unlikely to be                    Could reasonably be
explained by chance               explained by chance
          |                                 |
          +     -+     -+
                           v
          Now ask:
          - How large is the difference?
          - How certain are we? (Confidence interval)
          - Does the difference matter in practice?

Analysts often report a p-value when comparing two groups or evaluating an intervention.
A p-value helps us judge whether an observed difference is likely to be explained by chance alone.
A commonly used threshold is:







p-value
Interpretation




p < 0.05
The observed difference is unlikely to be explained by chance alone.


p ≥ 0.05
The observed difference could reasonably be explained by chance.



A p-value does not prove that a difference is real.
It simply helps us judge whether the observed difference is likely to be more than random variation.






ImportantWhat a P-value Doesn’t Tell Us



A p-value does not tell us:

how large the difference is
whether the difference is clinically or operationally important
whether we should change practice

A very small difference can still have a low p-value if enough data are available.
Likewise, a result that is not statistically significant may still be important, particularly when studies are small or evidence is limited.








TipAlways Consider



When interpreting a p-value, also ask:

How large is the difference?
How certain are we? (Look at the confidence interval.)
Does the difference matter in practice?
What are the costs, benefits and risks?


Statistical significance does not necessarily imply practical importance.




Example
A new intervention reduces hospital readmissions from 8.0% to 7.8%.
The analysis reports:

p = 0.01

The analysis suggests the observed 0.2% reduction is unlikely to be explained by chance alone.
However, it does not tell us whether a 0.2% reduction is:

clinically meaningful
cost-effective
sufficient to justify changing practice

Those decisions require consideration of the size of the difference, confidence intervals, costs, risks and the wider clinical context.


Poor Interpretation

“The p-value is greater than 0.05, so the intervention failed.”



Better Interpretation

“The evidence is uncertain. We should also consider the size of the difference, the confidence interval, the sample size and the wider context.



Poor Interpretation

“The difference is statistically significant, therefore it is important.”



Better Interpretation

“The difference is unlikely to be due to chance, but is it large enough to justify changing practice or investing further resources?”



Poor Interpretation

“The confidence intervals overlap, so there is definitely no difference.”



Better Interpretation

“Confidence intervals help us understand uncertainty, but they should be interpreted alongside the size of the difference, study design and the wider body of evidence.”
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
section: Risk of Action vs Risk of Inaction
text:
Risk of Action vs Risk of Inaction
When considering change, organisations often focus heavily on the risks of doing something.
However, every decision involves two sets of risks.

Risks of Action

Financial cost.
Opportunity cost.
Implementation challenges.
Unintended consequences.



Risks of Inaction

Continuing poor outcomes.
Increasing demand pressures.
Worsening inequalities.
Missed opportunities for improvement.

Sometimes the greatest risk is doing nothing.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Pragmatic Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
Not every decision requires the same level of evidence.
The level of evidence should be proportionate to the scale of risk.



Decision Type
Typical Evidence Requirement




Minor operational change
Local data and professional judgement


Small pilot
Local evaluation and benchmarking


Significant investment
Formal evaluation and business case


System-wide transformation
Strong evidence and ongoing evaluation



Waiting for perfect evidence can sometimes delay beneficial change unnecessarily.
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
A Practical Decision Framework
When faced with uncertainty, consider the following questions:

What do we know?
What do we not know?
What assumptions are being made?
What are the potential benefits?
What are the potential harms?
What happens if we delay?
Can we test the idea before scaling?

In many situations the answer is not “implement” or “do not implement”.
The answer is often:

“Pilot, evaluate, learn and adapt.”
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Poor Interpretation vs Better Interpretation

Poor Interpretation

“We don’t know for certain that this will work, so we should wait.”



Better Interpretation

“We have uncertainty, but do we have enough evidence to justify testing the intervention safely?”



Poor Interpretation

“The forecast says demand will increase by 15%.”



Better Interpretation

“The forecast suggests demand may increase by around 15%, but there is uncertainty around that estimate.”



Poor Interpretation

“The intervention might fail, so we shouldn’t proceed.”



Better Interpretation

“What are the risks of proceeding, and what are the risks of doing nothing?”



Poor Interpretation

“We need more data.”



Better Interpretation

“Would additional data materially change our decision?”
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Questions Decision-Makers Should Ask

What level of uncertainty exists in this analysis?
How much uncertainty surrounds this estimate?
Are the confidence intervals sufficiently narrow to support decision-making?
Is the result statistically significant, and more importantly, is it practically meaningful?
What assumptions underpin these findings?
What information is missing or unknown?
How sensitive are the conclusions to those assumptions?
What are the risks of acting?
What are the risks of not acting?
Is there a lower-risk way to test this first?
What evidence would increase our confidence?
Are we delaying action because of genuine uncertainty or because we are seeking certainty that may never exist?
Can we pilot, evaluate and adapt rather than committing to a full-scale implementation?
crumbs: 14  Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty

title: Module 10: Risk, Probability & Uncertainty
text:
Key Takeaways

Risk is not certainty.
Probability describes the likelihood of an event, not whether it will definitely occur.
All analyses contain some degree of uncertainty.
Confidence intervals communicate uncertainty around an estimate.
Statistical significance does not necessarily imply practical importance.
Forecasts and predictions should be interpreted as estimates rather than promises.
Decisions should consider both the risks of action and the risks of inaction.
Different decisions require different levels of evidence.
Waiting for perfect information is itself a decision and may carry risks.
Effective organisations acknowledge uncertainty, learn quickly and make proportionate decisions using the best evidence available at the time.

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
text:
Bringing Part 2 Together
Part 2 builds on the foundations of healthcare data literacy established in Part 1.
Understanding an individual statistic, chart or comparison is essential, but healthcare decisions rarely concern a single measure or service in isolation. Healthcare is a complex, interconnected system: patients move between services, demand and capacity change, populations have different needs, and interventions can influence outcomes across several pathways at once.
Part 2 therefore moves from interpreting healthcare data correctly to using evidence to understand systems, design improvements, evaluate interventions and make defensible decisions.
The ten modules explore:
Together, these modules help readers move beyond isolated performance measures or programme-level claims towards a more integrated understanding of need, flow, outcomes, implementation, equity, costs and value.
The modules in Part 2 are not standalone topics, nor do they represent a rigid sequence that every project must follow.
They provide complementary perspectives on the journey from understanding a healthcare problem to making a better-informed decision. In practice, teams may revisit earlier questions as new evidence emerges, data limitations become apparent or the proposed intervention changes.
crumbs: 16  Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
section: 1. Understand the system and establish a trustworthy evidence base
text:
1. Understand the system and establish a trustworthy evidence base
Modules 12–13
Demand, capacity and operational flow help explain why patients wait, where bottlenecks occur and how pressures in one part of a pathway affect another. Data quality and assurance help establish whether the information used to understand those pressures is sufficiently complete, consistent and fit for purpose.
A compelling dashboard or a rising activity trend is not, by itself, a reliable diagnosis of the problem. We need to understand both how the system operates and how confidently the data describe it.
crumbs: 16  Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
section: 2. Design better pathways and understand who they should serve
text:
2. Design better pathways and understand who they should serve
Modules 14 and 18
Pathway design considers how care could be organised differently, including the practical implications for implementation and evaluation. Population health management and segmentation help identify differing levels of need, complexity and risk, and where targeted approaches may be appropriate.
These perspectives should inform one another: the right intervention depends on the needs of the population, while the likely benefits depend on how the pathway is designed and delivered.
crumbs: 16  Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
section: 3. Evaluate impact, implementation and economic value
text:
3. Evaluate impact, implementation and economic value
Modules 15–17
Health economics introduces the questions of opportunity cost, outcomes and value. Applied economic methods help compare options and assess their costs and consequences. Evaluation of multiple interventions examines what changed, what may have contributed to that change, and why causal attribution is particularly challenging when services and patient populations overlap.
A reduction in hospital activity is not automatically evidence of better care or cash-releasing savings. Evaluation should also consider safety, patient and carer experience, equity, implementation fidelity, costs shifted between services and uncertainty about what would have happened otherwise.
The methodological foundations from Modules 7–9 in Part 1 remain important: a Theory of Change clarifies expected mechanisms, while appropriate evaluation designs help distinguish observed change from credible evidence of impact.
crumbs: 16  Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
section: 4. Explore future consequences before committing resources
text:
4. Explore future consequences before committing resources
Module 19
Scenario and simulation methods allow decision-makers to explore what might happen under different assumptions about demand, capacity, pathways, staffing or service configurations.
These methods can help identify trade-offs and unintended pressures before implementation. However, a simulation is only as useful as its assumptions, input data and validation; it is not proof that a proposed change will deliver the predicted result.
crumbs: 16  Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?

title: Part 2 — How do we understand, improve and evaluate complex healthcare systems?
section: 5. Bring evidence together and make a defensible decision
text:
5. Bring evidence together and make a defensible decision
Modules 20–21
Complex commissioning decisions rarely rest on one dataset or one method. Quantitative findings, qualitative evidence, published research, clinical and operational knowledge, economic analysis and the experiences of patients and communities may each illuminate different aspects of the problem.
Bringing evidence together means triangulating findings, explaining where sources agree or disagree, and being explicit about gaps and uncertainty. Moving from evidence to decision then requires judgement about benefits, harms, affordability, equity, opportunity costs and competing priorities.
The aim is not to remove judgement from healthcare decisions. It is to make that judgement better informed, transparent and open to challenge.






ImportantThe Big Picture



Good healthcare decisions rarely come from a single dataset, metric or analytical method.
They require us to ask:
What is happening across the system, and where are the pressures?
↓
Can we trust the data and understand its limitations?
↓
Whose needs are we trying to meet, and how should the pathway respond?
↓
What changed, what may have caused it, and was the intervention delivered as intended?
↓
What are the benefits, harms, costs, equity implications and opportunity costs?
↓
What could happen under different future scenarios?
↓
How do different forms of evidence fit together, and where do they disagree?
↓
What should we do next, given the trade-offs and uncertainty?
This is an iterative decision-making process, not a one-way checklist. New evidence may require us to revisit the problem, redesign the intervention or reconsider the decision.

title: Module 12: Demand, Capacity & Operational Flow
section: ⭐ Worked Example: Why Can the Waiting List Grow While RTT Performance Improves?
text:
⭐ Worked Example: Why Can the Waiting List Grow While RTT Performance Improves?
Imagine an NHS organisation successfully increases the number of first outpatient appointments available in an effort to improve access to elective care.
More patients are seen sooner following referral, resulting in:

more RTT clock starts
more patients entering the elective treatment pathway
improved access to specialist assessment

At first glance, this appears to be an unequivocal improvement.
However, if treatment capacity (for example, diagnostics, operating theatres or clinical workforce) does not increase at the same rate, more patients may enter the waiting list than leave it.
This creates an important system dynamic:

RTT clock starts represent patients entering the waiting list.
RTT clock finishes represent patients leaving the waiting list.

The size of the waiting list therefore depends on the balance between these two flows.

The waiting list behaves like a queue.
The waiting list is the stock, while RTT clock starts and RTT clock finishes are the flows into and out of that stock.
If RTT clock starts exceed RTT clock finishes, the waiting list grows.
If RTT clock finishes exceed RTT clock starts, the waiting list reduces.
The balance between these two flows determines whether the waiting list expands, contracts or remains stable.
One additional complexity is that organisations may improve their reported 18-week RTT performance by prioritising patients who are approaching the constitutional 18-week standard.
While this improves performance against the target, it does not necessarily reduce the overall waiting list if RTT clock starts continue to exceed RTT clock finishes.






ImportantKey Learning



Healthcare systems should be understood as interconnected stocks and flows, rather than as isolated performance measures.
Improving one performance metric does not necessarily mean the overall healthcare system has improved.
Understanding how patients enter, move through and leave the pathway is often more informative than looking at one performance indicator in isolation.
crumbs: 17  Module 12: Demand, Capacity & Operational Flow

title: Module 12: Demand, Capacity & Operational Flow
text:
Questions Decision-Makers Should Ask
Before concluding that elective performance has improved, ask:

Has referral demand increased?
Have first outpatient appointments increased?
Has treatment capacity increased by the same amount?
Are RTT clock finishes keeping pace with RTT clock starts?
Is the waiting list growing, shrinking or remaining stable?
Are we improving patient flow through the whole pathway, or simply optimising one part of it?
Which metric best reflects the performance of the whole pathway, rather than just one part of it?

Understanding the interaction between demand, capacity and patient flow provides a much richer picture of system performance than any single metric alone.
Looking at one performance measure in isolation may obscure important pressures elsewhere in the healthcare system.






TipLooking Beyond Elective Care



The same principles apply across many areas of healthcare.
Whether considering Emergency Departments, diagnostics, community services, mental health, cancer pathways or elective care, healthcare systems are fundamentally influenced by the interaction between demand, capacity and patient flow.
Understanding how patients enter, move through and leave a pathway often provides far greater insight than focusing on individual performance measures in isolation.
This systems perspective is one of the foundations of effective healthcare improvement.

title: Module 12: Demand, Capacity & Operational Flow
section: NHS Case Study: Delayed Discharge – A Whole-System Problem
text:
NHS Case Study: Delayed Discharge – A Whole-System Problem

Background
An acute hospital reports:

Emergency Department waiting times are increasing.
Ambulances are queuing outside the hospital.
Bed occupancy is consistently above 98%.
Elective operations are frequently cancelled.

The immediate assumption is:

The hospital needs more beds.



Initial Response
The organisation considers:

opening additional inpatient beds
increasing Emergency Department staffing
recruiting more ward nurses

Each of these actions may provide short-term relief.
However, several months later, performance remains largely unchanged.


Looking Deeper
Further investigation reveals that many patients are medically fit for discharge, but cannot leave hospital because:

community rehabilitation capacity is limited
social care packages are unavailable
community nursing services are under pressure

As a result:

beds remain occupied unnecessarily
new admissions cannot move from the Emergency Department onto wards
Emergency Department cubicles remain full
ambulances cannot offload patients promptly

The apparent hospital capacity problem is actually a patient flow problem.
Increasing inpatient beds without improving discharge processes may simply increase the number of occupied beds rather than improving patient flow.


Understanding the System
The visible pressure occurs in the Emergency Department.
The underlying constraint lies much further downstream.
Improving discharge capacity may release considerably more effective hospital capacity than simply opening additional inpatient beds.
This illustrates an important systems principle:

The constraint is not always where the pressure is most visible.



Applying Systems Thinking
Rather than asking:

“How do we create more beds?”

decision-makers might instead ask:

What is preventing timely discharge?
Which patients experience the longest delays?
Which organisations influence discharge?
Would investment in community services have a greater system-wide impact?
Are we solving the bottleneck—or simply moving it elsewhere?



Lessons Learned
This example demonstrates that:

operational pressure is often caused by poor patient flow rather than insufficient capacity
bottlenecks create queues throughout the healthcare system
increasing resources where pressure is most visible may not address the underlying constraint
effective improvement requires understanding the entire patient pathway rather than individual services in isolation







TipLeadership Reflection



The greatest pressure within a healthcare system is not always where the underlying problem originates.
As a leader, ask yourself:
If I remove pressure here, have I solved the underlying constraint—or simply moved the pressure elsewhere?








ImportantThe Big Picture



Looking at one performance measure in isolation may obscure important pressures elsewhere in the healthcare system.
Understanding how demand, capacity and patient flow interact is fundamental to improving healthcare systems.

From Data to Evidence
Data alone is not evidence.

What was recorded

Can we trust it?

Problems introduced early in this journey can influence everything that follows.

Similarly, a beautifully designed dashboard may create false confidence if the underlying data are incomplete, poorly defined or misunderstood.

7. Fitness for Purpose

ImportantMissing Data Can Introduce Bias

If particular populations, services or geographical areas are systematically less well represented, the resulting analysis may provide an incomplete picture of need or outcomes.
A dataset can therefore appear broadly complete while still being less reliable for particular groups.
When assessing completeness, ask not only:

title: Module 13: Data Quality, Assurance & Trustworthy Data
text:
Why This Matters for Attribution
Once a patient moves between wards, specialties or consultants, another question arises:

Who should the patient’s activity or outcome be attributed to?

Should a 14-day hospital stay be attributed to:

the specialty that admitted the patient?
the specialty that discharged the patient?
the service responsible for most of their care?
each consultant episode separately?
each ward according to the time spent there?

There may not always be one universally correct answer.
The appropriate approach depends on the question being asked.
What matters is that the definition and attribution method are understood, applied consistently and clearly communicated.
This leads to another important data literacy principle:

The same patient journey can produce different analytical answers depending on what is counted and how it is attributed.
crumbs: 18  Module 13: Data Quality, Assurance & Trustworthy Data

title: Module 13: Data Quality, Assurance & Trustworthy Data
section: Why This Matters for Performance Comparisons
text:
Why This Matters for Performance Comparisons
Suppose one hospital reports average length of stay by admitting specialty, while another attributes patients according to their discharging specialty.
A direct comparison may appear valid.
But the organisations may not actually be measuring the same thing.
Similarly, changes in attribution methodology over time can create apparent improvements or deterioration even when the underlying patient experience has not changed.
This is why analytical assurance should consider not only whether the numbers are technically correct, but whether the method used to produce them is appropriate and consistent.






TipQuestions Decision-Makers Should Ask



When reviewing performance attributed to a service, specialty or organisation, ask:

What exactly is being attributed?
What is the unit of analysis: patient, spell, episode or ward stay?
Is activity attributed to the starting or ending service?
How are patients who move between specialties handled?
Are the same attribution rules being used across organisations?
Have the attribution rules changed over time?
Would using a different attribution method materially change the conclusion?

Always understand who gets the number — and why before drawing conclusions from it.
crumbs: 18  Module 13: Data Quality, Assurance & Trustworthy Data

title: Module 13: Data Quality, Assurance & Trustworthy Data
text:
A Practical Data Assurance Checklist
Before relying on important analysis, ask:

Has the underlying data been validated?
Are the definitions clearly documented?
Is the source of the data understood?
Have known limitations been clearly stated?
Have unexpected results or unusual trends been investigated?
Can the analysis be reproduced?
Has the analytical methodology been documented?
Has the methodology been reviewed by someone appropriately skilled?
Has the output been sense-checked by people who understand the service or pathway?
Is there an appropriate audit trail?
Is there a clear owner accountable for the data?
Is the level of assurance proportionate to the importance of the decision?







ImportantAssurance Is Not Just an Analytical Responsibility



Trustworthy information often requires collaboration between:

analysts
clinicians
operational teams
data engineers
information governance teams
clinical coders
data owners
data stewards

The people closest to the service or pathway often provide essential context that cannot be identified from the data alone.
A number can be technically valid while still failing to reflect what is happening operationally.
