text:
7. Construct a Credible Counterfactual
Section 6 established that the reported 8% reduction in emergency admissions is descriptive, not proof of impact. We now ask what would have happened to the eligible frailty population had the integrated portfolio not been introduced.
The following worked example uses a separate, entirely hypothetical set of admission counts and rates to demonstrate the reasoning. Its numerical results are not derived from the preceding 8% observation or from the later illustrative portfolio estimate of 470 admissions.






ImportantThe central evaluation question



Emergency admissions among people living with frailty have fallen following the introduction of an integrated model of care. How many admissions would we have expected if that model had not been introduced?



7.1 Why the Counterfactual Matters
An observed change is not necessarily an intervention effect. A counterfactual is the outcome that would have occurred for the same eligible population, during the same period, under a specified alternative, such as continuation of the previous model of care.
We cannot observe both the intervention and no-intervention outcomes for the same population at the same time. This is the fundamental problem of causal inference. Evaluation designs therefore attempt to estimate the unobserved outcome using defensible assumptions and available data.
For an Integrated Care Board (ICB), the primary question might be whether the combined integrated frailty model improved outcomes for the population it was designed to serve—not how many admissions each constituent service can individually claim to have prevented.


7.2 Worked Example: Frailty Admissions
Suppose an ICB introduces proactive frailty management, enhanced care home support, Urgent Community Response, virtual wards and neighbourhood multidisciplinary teams in 2025. The services operate together, but not every eligible person receives every component.
In 2026, the eligible cohort experiences 900 emergency admissions. An evaluation estimates that 1,100 admissions would have occurred under continuation of the previous care model.
\[
\text{Estimated admissions avoided}=1{,}100-900=200
\]
The corresponding estimated relative difference is:
\[
\frac{900-1{,}100}{1{,}100}\times100\approx-18.2\%.
\]
These are illustrative figures, not findings from an actual ICB evaluation. The calculation is straightforward; the difficult task is establishing whether 1,100 is a credible counterfactual.






NoteCounts, rates and population changes



If the size or composition of the eligible cohort changes, comparing admission counts alone can mislead. Define the estimand first: for example, total admissions attributable to the policy in a specified population and period, or emergency admissions per 1,000 person-years. Where appropriate, account for age, frailty severity, multimorbidity and deprivation. The adjustment strategy must follow the causal question.




7.3 Visualising the Unobserved Alternative
The chart below uses hypothetical annual data to illustrate observed admissions and an estimated no-intervention trajectory. The counterfactual is modelled, not observed.

Line chart of annual emergency admissions from 2022 to 2026. Observed admissions decline to 900 in 2026, while the illustrative no-intervention counterfactual reaches 1,100.
A widening gap may represent an intervention effect only if the assumptions used to estimate the no-intervention trajectory are credible. Other changes—population need, hospital capacity, clinical thresholds or wider policy—could also explain it.


7.4 Define the Population and the Effect of Interest
Before selecting a statistical method, specify:

Eligibility: Who qualifies as part of the frailty population, using which definition and at what date?
Intervention: What does the integrated model comprise, when did it begin and how consistently was it implemented?
Comparator: What would care have looked like without the model—for example, continuation of previous arrangements?
Outcome: Emergency admissions, bed days, patient-reported outcomes, experience, functional status, equity or a combination?
Time horizon: Over what period might benefits or harms plausibly emerge?
Estimand: Are we estimating the effect of offering or implementing the model for the eligible population, or the effect of actually receiving a particular component?


Fixed and Dynamic Cohorts Answer Different Questions
A fixed baseline cohort follows everyone eligible at a defined starting point. This can clarify outcomes among those eligible when the policy began, but the cohort ages and experiences deaths and other changes over time.
A dynamic eligible population includes people as they become eligible. It may better reflect ongoing commissioning responsibility, but changing cohort membership and case mix require careful handling.
Do not restrict the primary cohort to people who used the new services: uptake may depend on health status, access or clinical judgement, introducing selection bias. Also avoid excluding people who died or only analysing survivors without considering the consequences.



7.5 Constructing a Credible Comparison








Approach
What it attempts
Main assumptions and risks




Historical trend projection
Extends the pre-intervention pattern into the post-intervention period
The pre-existing relationship must remain relevant; other time-varying changes can distort the estimate


Interrupted Time Series (ITS)
Estimates a change in outcome level and/or trend at implementation
Requires enough observations, appropriate modelling of seasonality and autocorrelation, and no unaccounted concurrent changes driving the result


Controlled ITS
Compares the intervention series with a comparison series over time
Comparison must represent relevant shared pressures without being substantially affected by the intervention


Difference-in-Differences (DiD)
Compares changes in intervention and comparison populations
Requires a credible parallel-trends assumption for untreated potential outcomes, with attention to differing trends, spillovers and timing


Randomised or stepped-wedge design
Uses random allocation or randomised rollout to construct a comparison
Requires feasible and ethical allocation, careful attention to timing, contamination and analysis of clustered data



No method is automatically causal because of its name. Design quality, data completeness, implementation timing and the plausibility of assumptions matter more than technical sophistication.

Interrupted Time Series: Did the Level or Trend Change?
With sufficiently frequent pre- and post-intervention observations, segmented regression can estimate an immediate level change and a change in slope:
\[
Y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1t+\beta_2I_t+\beta_3(t-T_0)I_t+\varepsilon_t,
\]
where \(I_t\) indicates the post-implementation period and \(T_0\) is the implementation time. Here, \(\beta_2\) represents an immediate level change and \(\beta_3\) a change in trend, under the model assumptions.
In frailty care, implementation may be gradual rather than instantaneous. It may be more realistic to model a phased rollout, a delayed effect or a transition period. Seasonality, autocorrelation and changes in eligible population size must also be considered.
Key limitation: An ITS without a control cannot reliably distinguish the intervention from another event occurring at the same time.


Controlled ITS and Difference-in-Differences: What Does a Comparison Add?
Suppose a comparable area did not introduce the same integrated frailty model during the evaluation period. Its trend may help represent shared pressures such as winter demand or national policy changes.
A simple DiD illustration uses rates per 1,000 person-years, not raw counts:



Population
Before
After
Change




Integrated frailty model area
300
260
−40


Comparison area
280
270
−10



\[
\text{DiD estimate}=(-40)-(-10)=-30
\]
Under credible assumptions, this suggests 30 fewer emergency admissions per 1,000 person-years than expected without the model. It does not imply that the intervention area’s admission rate would otherwise have equalled the comparison area’s rate.
For DiD, the key assumption is that, without the intervention, the change in outcomes would have been comparable between groups. Similar baseline levels alone are insufficient. Examine multiple pre-intervention periods, case mix, policy changes, spillovers and differences in implementation. Pre-trend checks are informative but cannot prove the assumption.
Where treatment starts at different times in different areas, use methods suited to staggered adoption rather than assuming a conventional two-way fixed-effects estimate is always appropriate.



7.6 Why Frailty Makes Causal Evaluation Harder


Changing population need
Age-standardisation alone may not account for shifts in frailty severity, multimorbidity, deprivation or the proportion approaching end of life. However, do not automatically adjust for every available variable: adjusting for a factor changed by the intervention can remove part of the effect being estimated. Distinguish baseline confounders from potential mediators.


Regression to the mean
Patients are often identified following unusually high hospital use. Some reduction may occur naturally even without additional care. A simple before-and-after comparison among high users can therefore overstate impact.


Confounding by indication
Patients receiving intensive support may have greater underlying need than those receiving less. Worse outcomes in the intensively supported group do not necessarily imply that the service was harmful; conversely, better outcomes among participants may reflect selection.


Mortality and competing events
Death changes a person’s opportunity to be admitted. Analyse mortality alongside utilisation, consider person-time and competing-event approaches where relevant, and avoid reporting lower admission rates as unequivocally positive without examining survival and wellbeing.


Concurrent changes and spillovers
Workforce constraints, discharge policies, coding practices, admission thresholds and other service developments may change at the same time. Comparison areas may also adopt similar practices or experience indirect effects, weakening their value as untreated controls.


Implementation is not a single date
An integrated model may expand gradually across neighbourhoods, with changing staffing, eligibility and uptake. Record implementation milestones and actual reach. Treating the first announcement date as a precise intervention boundary may be misleading.


7.7 Test the Counterfactual Assumptions
Counterfactual estimates are uncertain. One practical teaching exercise is to ask how conclusions change under different plausible assumptions.









Illustrative scenario
Expected admissions without the model
Observed admissions
Estimated difference




Conservative
950
900
50 fewer


Central
1,100
900
200 fewer


Higher-demand
1,200
900
300 fewer



These figures are scenarios, not confidence intervals. In a real evaluation, report model-based uncertainty and undertake sensitivity analyses appropriate to the design—for example, alternative trend specifications, comparison groups, intervention dates, case-mix adjustment and outcome definitions.
The commissioning question is not simply whether the estimate is statistically significant. It is also: Would our decision to sustain or expand the model change if the true benefit were much smaller than the central estimate?


7.8 A Counterfactual Is Not Just a Forecast
A forecast asks, What is likely to happen? A causal counterfactual asks, What would happen under a specified alternative policy or care arrangement?
Both may use statistical modelling, but the counterfactual requires explicit assumptions about the alternative intervention and the causes of the outcome. A model that accurately predicts admissions does not, by itself, establish the causal effect of integrated care.
This distinction becomes particularly important when linking evaluation with scenarios and simulation in Module 19.


7.9 What If the Scheme Has Already Started and No Counterfactual Was Planned?
In NHS practice, evaluation is frequently requested after a pathway, service or integrated model has begun. The business case may describe expected benefits, but nobody may have specified a comparison group, preserved a pre-implementation baseline or recorded consistent implementation dates.
This does not automatically mean that causal evaluation is impossible. A counterfactual is an unobserved alternative outcome, not necessarily a control group recruited before implementation. In some circumstances it can be estimated retrospectively. In others, no defensible estimate is available, and the evaluation must answer more limited—but still useful—questions.






ImportantThe Principle





No counterfactual planned is not the same as no counterfactual possible. First assess whether a credible comparison can be reconstructed. If not, do not invent one: evaluate implementation, reach, outcomes, experience and plausible contribution, and design stronger evaluation around the next decision.




Worked example: Integrated frailty care introduced in April 2024
Imagine the ICB introduced its integrated frailty model in April 2024. It is now October 2026. Commissioners want to know whether the model has reduced emergency admissions, but no prospective evaluation design was agreed.
The team starts with a retrospective evaluability assessment, not with a preferred statistical method:

Clarify the decision. Is the ICB deciding whether to continue the model, expand it, change eligibility or redesign particular components?
Specify the intervention and alternative. What actually changed in April 2024, when did each component become operational, and what care would have been provided without it?
Define the eligible population. Can severe frailty eligibility be reconstructed consistently before and after implementation? Were criteria or coding changed by the scheme itself?
Inventory the data. What historical monthly outcomes, denominators, case-mix measures, implementation records and patient/carer evidence exist?
Look for credible comparisons. Were similar localities unaffected, or was rollout staggered? Did other changes occur at the same time?
Agree what claims are supportable. Record limitations before results are known and identify what further evidence could change the commissioning decision.



Scenario A: Historical data can be reconstructed
Suppose monthly admissions data are available from April 2021 and the eligible frailty population can be identified consistently. The team may conduct a retrospective ITS, comparing observed post-April-2024 admissions with a modelled continuation of the pre-intervention pattern.
This is only credible if the pre-intervention observations are sufficient to characterise trends and seasonality, the intervention timing is meaningful, outcome definitions remain comparable, and important concurrent changes are investigated. Serial correlation, changing population size, frailty severity and mortality also need consideration.
If suitable comparison areas exist, a controlled ITS or Difference-in-Differences design may strengthen the evaluation. However, comparison areas must be assessed for differences in baseline need, prior trends, service changes and spillovers. A neighbouring ICB is not automatically a valid control.
Where eligibility is only recorded because patients entered the new service, the analyst must not treat the post-implementation recipient list as though it were an unbiased historical frailty cohort. Doing so can introduce selection bias. A consistent, pre-specified population definition—or a clearly stated alternative estimand—is needed.
Possible conclusion: “Following introduction of the integrated frailty model, admissions were lower than estimated under the specified counterfactual trend, subject to assumptions about concurrent changes and cohort comparability.”
This conclusion is stronger than a simple before-and-after comparison, but does not automatically identify the causal effect of each component.


Scenario B: Only post-implementation data are available
Now suppose reliable records begin in April 2024, the historical eligible cohort cannot be reconstructed and no defensible comparison population exists.
The ICB cannot reliably estimate admissions avoided by the original introduction from these data alone. A reduction in admissions among people using the pathway is not evidence that those admissions would otherwise have occurred.
The evaluation can instead ask:

Reach and equity: Who was eligible, referred, accepted and treated? Which neighbourhoods or groups are underrepresented?
Implementation: Was the model delivered as intended, with sufficient staffing, timely access and coordination between services?
Outcomes and safety: What admission rates, patient-reported experiences, functional outcomes, adverse events and unintended consequences are observed?
Mechanisms: Do shared care plans, rapid response and clinical coordination operate as expected in the Theory of Change?
Alternative explanations: Could coding changes, admission thresholds, other pathways, changing need or capacity constraints explain the observed patterns?
Decision relevance: What is working operationally, what should change, and which uncertainties matter most before further investment?

Qualitative interviews, pathway audits, patient/carer accounts and implementation records are important here. They can explain experiences and test whether expected mechanisms are plausible, but triangulation does not turn a descriptive study into a causal impact estimate.
Possible conclusion: “The evaluation identifies improvements in coordination and reported experience, alongside gaps in access and delivery. It cannot determine how many admissions were prevented by the original introduction of the model.”


Scenario C: Use the next change as an evaluation opportunity
The ICB is now considering expanding the integrated model to additional neighbourhoods or strengthening the connection between proactive frailty care and UCR.
Although the original introduction cannot be evaluated causally with confidence, the incremental effect of the proposed change may be evaluable prospectively.
Before implementation, the team can:

Define the new decision, eligibility criteria, outcomes and intended mechanisms.
Record a common baseline for participating and potential comparison areas.
Agree implementation dates and measure actual uptake and intensity.
Consider a phased rollout, controlled comparison or randomised allocation only where feasible, ethical and operationally appropriate.
Pre-specify how changing need, mortality, contamination and concurrent service changes will be handled.
Include patient/carer experience, implementation fidelity, costs, equity and unintended consequences.
Agree review points and what findings would justify continuation, redesign or wider expansion.

The causal question is now “What additional difference did the expansion or redesign make compared with continuing the existing model?” It is not “What was the total historical impact of the original portfolio?”


Which evaluation route is feasible?









Evidence situation
Practical approach
Appropriate claim
Avoid claiming




Consistent historical outcomes and a clear implementation point
Retrospective ITS with sensitivity analyses
Estimated change relative to a modelled no-change trend, conditional on assumptions
That all contemporaneous changes were caused by the scheme


Suitable comparison population or phased implementation
Controlled ITS, DiD or other appropriate comparative design
A comparative impact estimate if design assumptions are credible
That geographic proximity guarantees comparability


Patient-level eligibility, timing and outcomes available
Longitudinal analysis, potentially with causal methods
An estimate for a clearly specified population and intervention contrast, subject to confounding assumptions
That adjustment automatically removes selection bias


Post-implementation data only, no credible comparison
Descriptive, implementation and qualitative evaluation
Reach, observed outcomes, experiences, mechanisms and plausible contribution
A precise number of admissions avoided


Further expansion or redesign is planned
Prospectively designed evaluation of the next change
Incremental effect of the change, if a credible design is implemented
Retrospective proof of the original model’s impact





Contribution analysis when attribution is not feasible
A structured theory-based contribution analysis can still be useful when causal identification is weak. It asks whether the intervention was implemented, whether the expected mechanisms operated, whether observed changes fit the Theory of Change, and how well alternative explanations have been investigated.
For example, shared frailty care plans may help UCR clinicians treat suitable patients at home. Evidence might include documented care-plan availability, staff accounts, patient experiences and referral-to-response times. This can support a plausible contribution narrative, especially if contradictory findings are actively examined.
It cannot, on its own, tell the ICB that the model prevented a specific number of emergency admissions. Similarly, benchmarking against a national average provides context but is not automatically a causal comparison.






TipA Practical Reporting Rule





Use distinct language for distinct evidence:

Observed change: “Emergency admissions fell after implementation.”
Comparative estimate: “Admissions were lower than the estimated counterfactual, under the stated assumptions.”
Plausible contribution: “Implementation and qualitative evidence support the model’s contribution to improved coordination.”
Unresolved causal impact: “The effect of the original implementation on admissions cannot be estimated reliably from the available data.”

The absence of a defensible counterfactual does not mean abandoning evaluation. It means changing the question and being clear about the answer.






7.10 From Estimated Impact to a Commissioning Decision
Even a credible cohort-level estimate cannot by itself tell us why the model worked, which components mattered, whether benefits were equitable, or whether the outcomes justified the investment.
A rounded assessment draws on four complementary perspectives:

Impact: How did outcomes differ from the estimated counterfactual?
Explanation: What do pathway analysis, implementation evidence and patient/carer experiences suggest about how and why change occurred?
Value: Were incremental benefits worth the resources used, including opportunity costs? Released capacity is not necessarily a cash-releasing saving.
Equity: Which groups benefited, which did not, and did inequalities narrow or widen?

Patient-level pathway analysis can help explain patterns of care, but should not be confused with an unbiased estimate of the causal effect of receiving a particular component. Where commissioners need to choose between components, targeted evaluations may be necessary.






TipQuestions to take into an evaluation planning meeting




What exactly is our eligible frailty population, and how will it change over time?
What care would have continued without the integrated model?
What other changes might affect admissions during the same period?
Is there a credible comparison population, or enough repeated observations for ITS?
How will we handle mortality, changing need and regression to the mean?
Which assumptions would most change the estimated impact?
What qualitative, equity and economic evidence is needed to interpret the result?





Match the Strength of the Claim to the Evidence
A proportionate assurance framework helps commissioners understand what an evaluation can support. These are illustrative assurance categories, not universal standards or guarantees of causality.








Assurance
Illustrative evidence
What the ICB may reasonably conclude




Bronze
Aggregate trends, programme activity, implementation accounts and qualitative evidence
What changed, who was reached and which contributions are plausible; not an attributed impact estimate


Silver
More reliable exposure data, baseline-risk adjustment, a defensible comparator where available, plus implementation evidence
A more informative estimate of possible impact, conditional on comparability and other assumptions


Gold
A credible quasi-experimental or other strong evaluation design, appropriate longitudinal analysis and triangulation
Stronger causal conclusions about the portfolio or clearly distinguishable changes, where the design genuinely identifies them



A complex model does not automatically produce Gold evidence. Simultaneous roll-out of several interventions may prevent separate causal estimates even with excellent linked data. Assurance should be assessed for each claim, including the claim that an alternative configuration would deliver additional benefit.






TipHow Much Evidence Is Enough?





Ask: What could go wrong if we act now, how reversible is the decision, and which missing evidence could realistically change it? A low-cost reversible improvement may justify proportionate monitoring; a major irreversible reallocation needs more demanding scrutiny.

section: 8. Examine Combinations, Not Just Individual Services
text:
8. Examine Combinations, Not Just Individual Services
The team maps patient exposure to meaningful combinations of care, rather than attempting every possible combination of five interventions regardless of sample size.
Keep the questions distinct: the primary cohort-level evaluation estimates the impact of offering or implementing the integrated model. Patient-level pathway comparisons can illuminate how care was delivered and possible mechanisms, but they do not automatically identify the causal effect of each component, particularly when exposure depends on changing clinical need.
For example:







Exposure group
Question




Neither proactive frailty care nor UCR
What happened under other existing care arrangements?


Frailty care only
What changes followed proactive support?


UCR only
What changes followed rapid response?


Frailty care and UCR
Is there evidence that proactive support enabled more effective crisis response?



These groups are not automatically comparable. Some combinations may be rare or clinically inappropriate for particular patients. Exposure also changes over time, so an analyst may need methods that handle time-varying treatment and confounding.
Interventions may be:

Independent: each produces effects through largely separate mechanisms.
Complementary: one increases the effectiveness of another.
Sequential: one enables a later stage of care.
Substitutive: one provides an alternative to another.
Duplicative: two services provide substantially overlapping activity without additional benefit.

An intervention with a small apparent isolated effect may nevertheless be important if it enables another service to work effectively. Conversely, overlapping services may create duplication or double-running costs.

Illustrative Interaction—Not an Impact Estimate
Imagine separate, credible analyses eventually suggest different outcomes for patients receiving proactive frailty care, UCR or both. The combination could perform differently from the sum of the individual effects because early planning enables rapid response.
This possibility should be tested, not assumed. Simply comparing crude outcomes across exposure groups cannot establish synergy because those groups may differ in risk, timing and clinical need.

section: 9. Triangulate Quantitative, Qualitative and Implementation Evidence
text:
9. Triangulate Quantitative, Qualitative and Implementation Evidence
Numbers alone may not explain how the portfolio works. The team combines:

Quantitative evidence: outcome trends, comparisons, reach, timing, variation and uncertainty.
Qualitative evidence: patient and carer experience, professional perspectives, barriers and unintended effects.
Implementation evidence: referral criteria, staffing, fidelity, capacity, actual uptake and coordination between services.
Theory of Change: whether the proposed mechanisms occurred in practice.

For example, interviews may reveal that UCR works more effectively when patients already have an accessible frailty care plan. Alternatively, they may show that overlapping referral routes delay access. Neither finding alone proves an effect on admissions, but both help explain observed patterns and identify what should be tested or redesigned.
A useful conclusion might be:

The available comparative, implementation and qualitative evidence is consistent with proactive frailty care and UCR making complementary contributions to the observed improvement, although their separate causal effects remain uncertain.

The strength of the wording must match the evidence.

Was the Integrated Model Delivered as Intended?
A null or disappointing outcome does not, by itself, establish that the underlying care model is ineffective. The ICB first distinguishes failure of the intervention theory from failure to implement or reach the intended population.
The evaluation should record:








Implementation question
Evidence to collect
Why it changes interpretation




Reach — who was offered support?
Eligible, referred, accepted and treated populations; reasons for non-participation
Low reach may dilute population-level impact and conceal inequitable access


Fidelity — was the model delivered?
Care plans completed, MDT participation, response times and delivery against core service specifications
An intervention that was not delivered as designed is not a clean test of its theory


Dose and duration — how much support occurred?
Number, timing and intensity of contacts; time from referral to first intervention
A single contact may not represent the intended longitudinal pathway


Capacity and context — what constrained delivery?
Staffing, vacancies, caseloads, local service availability and referral bottlenecks
Implementation can vary with demand and operational pressure


Integration — did components connect?
Shared plans, handovers, referrals between frailty care and UCR, and clinician/patient accounts
Benefits may depend on coordination rather than on individual components alone


Adaptation — did the model change?
Dates and reasons for changes in eligibility, staffing, pathways and operating hours
A single implementation date may conceal several different versions of the intervention



Interpretation example (illustrative): suppose the portfolio-level analysis finds no clear reduction in admissions. Implementation records reveal that only 35% of the eligible population received a completed frailty review, and UCR access varied considerably by locality. The result may indicate that the portfolio as implemented did not demonstrate the intended population-level effect. It does not establish that full and equitable delivery would have been ineffective.
The reverse is also true: high fidelity does not prove the model works. If delivery was strong but outcomes did not improve, the ICB should scrutinise the Theory of Change, time horizon, measures, comparator and plausible unintended effects.






TipKeep implementation and causal questions separate



Implementation evidence helps explain what was delivered, to whom and under what conditions. It can support a contribution argument and guide redesign, but differences between high- and low-exposure patients should not be interpreted as causal dose–response effects without addressing selection and time-varying confounding. See Module 9.




When the Evidence Disagrees
Imagine the comparative analysis suggests that the frailty portfolio is associated with fewer emergency admissions. However, patient interviews describe delays and inconsistent continuity, while UCR staff report that referrals often exceed available capacity. Analysis also suggests that people in more deprived neighbourhoods are less likely to receive proactive frailty assessment.
These findings are not resolved by taking an average or privileging whichever result supports the original business case. The team investigates whether improvements are concentrated in some localities or groups, whether access and implementation differ, and whether the outcome measures overlook important experiences.
A defensible synthesis could conclude that some evidence supports an improvement in hospital activity, but access, delivery and patient-experience concerns limit confidence in the portfolio’s overall value. It should specify what further analysis or service improvement is needed. Module 20 develops broader evidence synthesis in greater depth.


Test Whether Benefits Are Equitably Distributed
For the severe frailty cohort, compare eligible population → referred → accepted → actually treated → outcomes, by locality and relevant characteristics such as deprivation, living arrangements and care home status. For people approaching the end of life, assess preference-concordant outcomes separately.
A fall in admissions at ICB level can coexist with unequal access. For example, lower uptake in deprived neighbourhoods might reflect unmet need, different eligibility, patient preferences or incomplete recording. The evaluation must investigate rather than assume the explanation. These findings feed into the population analysis developed further in Module 18.

section: 10. Reconcile Programme Claims and Avoid Double-Counting
text:
10. Reconcile Programme Claims and Avoid Double-Counting
Suppose three programme reports present the following illustrative estimates:



Programme
Claimed avoided emergency admissions




Proactive frailty care
250


UCR
300


Virtual wards
200


Sum of programme claims
750



These numbers should not automatically be added. They may arise from different counterfactual assumptions, overlapping populations, different time periods or the same underlying pathway change.
Suppose a separate, credible portfolio-level evaluation estimates 470 fewer admissions than the counterfactual, with appropriate uncertainty. The ICB now has two distinct findings: programme claims total 750, while the portfolio estimate is 470.
This does not prove that exactly 280 admissions were double-counted. Differences may also reflect methods, populations, time periods and uncertainty. Nor does deduplicating patient records reveal the number of admissions avoided: an avoided admission is a counterfactual event, not an observed record.
The team therefore reconciles definitions and methods, identifies overlapping claims and reports the portfolio-level estimate separately. It does not allocate the 470 among programmes unless the design supports that attribution.






ImportantOne Outcome Cannot Be Claimed Several Times





Adding programme-level avoided-activity estimates is not a valid portfolio impact estimate when interventions overlap. First establish whether the estimates measure compatible effects, populations and periods; then use the strongest defensible portfolio analysis.




A Financial Caution
Multiplying 470 estimated avoided admissions by an average admission cost may illustrate the notional value of activity, but does not automatically demonstrate a cash-releasing saving. Staff, beds and estate may remain in place, while capacity is used for other patients.
Similarly, do not add monetised ED, admission and bed-day benefits if these measures represent overlapping consequences of the same episode. The economic assessment needs consistent boundaries and a clear account of what has—and has not—been counted.

section: 11. Bring the Findings into a STAR-Informed Portfolio Review
text:
11. Bring the Findings into a STAR-Informed Portfolio Review
Module 16 introduces the Socio-Technical Allocation of Resources (STAR) approach and its methods. Module 17 applies the principles to a more complicated situation: the effectiveness and value of one intervention may depend on the presence of another.
The ICB brings together commissioners, finance, health economics, analysts, providers, clinicians, patients and carers to consider realistic alternative configurations, not simply a list of programmes competing in isolation.







Portfolio option
Question for the evidence review




Maintain the current portfolio
What outcomes, resource requirements and uncertainties are associated with current arrangements?


Expand proactive frailty care
Which additional patients could benefit, and what incremental effect is plausible?


Strengthen frailty care and UCR together
Is there evidence that the combination delivers additional benefit?


Target virtual wards differently
Would revised eligibility improve outcomes or resource use without excluding people who benefit?


Improve coordination with end-of-life care
Could better integration improve preference-concordant care and reduce unwanted transfers?



For each feasible option, the team assembles the relevant STAR-style inputs: population who could benefit, incremental resource requirements, expected incremental health benefit, uncertainty and the alternatives forgone. Where possible, the analysis estimates the additional effect of the proposed portfolio change, not the sum of standalone programme claims.
This matters because an independence assumption may be inappropriate when interventions are complementary, sequential or duplicative. If the evidence cannot quantify interactions credibly, the limitation should be explicit and tested through scenarios rather than hidden in a single precise figure.
The review also considers distributional effects and outcomes that are difficult to reduce to one metric, particularly preference-concordant end-of-life care. STAR-informed discussion helps stakeholders examine evidence and trade-offs; it does not replace their judgement or automatically determine a commissioning decision.

Worked Comparison: What Would Change from Today’s Portfolio?
Suppose the ICB’s existing portfolio costs £4.0 million annually. The portfolio evaluation reports an illustrative estimate of 470 fewer emergency admissions than its counterfactual, with substantial uncertainty. This is a portfolio-level historical estimate, not the incremental benefit of any new proposal.
For the next planning year, the team considers three scenarios. The figures below are hypothetical planning assumptions to demonstrate how evidence would be assembled; they are not STAR outputs, evaluated effects, recommendations or additive benefit claims. The health-benefit estimates are expressed in illustrative additional quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) only where meaningful and sufficiently measurable. End-of-life experience and preference-concordant care are reported alongside them, not treated as equivalent to avoided admissions.










Scenario versus current arrangements
Additional annual cost
Additional people reached
Illustrative incremental health benefit
Key uncertainty or dependency




A. Maintain existing portfolio
£0

Existing benefits and delivery pressures still need monitoring


B. Expand frailty care and integrate UCR
£450,000
600
25–55 additional QALYs if the combined pathway works as modelled
UCR staffing, access to care plans, selection of patients and possible interaction effects


C. Retarget virtual wards and coordinate end-of-life care
£250,000
350
10–35 additional QALYs for outcomes suitably captured by QALYs
Clinical eligibility, safe alternatives and how preference-concordant care is measured



How to read this table: All costs, reach and benefits are incremental relative to A. The QALY ranges are assumed scenarios to be populated by a health economist using defensible evidence, not inferred from the 470 avoided admissions. The ranges do not constitute confidence intervals. B and C may reach some of the same people, so their costs and benefits cannot simply be added to describe a combined option.
The team should first test whether each option is clinically appropriate and deliverable. It then checks the evidence for the estimated incremental health benefit, identifies who gains or loses access, and tests sensitivity to uptake, staffing, unit costs and intervention interactions. STAR methods covered in Module 16 can then help structure the comparison and facilitated deliberation.

section: A Decision Conference, Not an Automatic Winner
text:
A Decision Conference, Not an Automatic Winner
The workshop might find that B has greater potential population reach but relies on additional UCR capacity; C has a lower stated incremental cost but important uncertainty about the right outcomes for end-of-life patients. Participants may request revised eligibility, a phased implementation, more robust evidence or a new combined scenario. The numbers alone cannot settle the choice, particularly when equity, patient preferences and interactions matter.

section: 12. What If Linked Patient-Level Data Are Unavailable?
text:
12. What If Linked Patient-Level Data Are Unavailable?
The absence of linked data should change the strength of the conclusions, not prevent all useful evaluation. Likewise, a scheme that began without an evaluation plan may still be assessed retrospectively if credible historical or comparison data exist (see Section 7.9).
The team can begin with aggregate trends, service activity, implementation dates, variation across places, published evidence, available hospital and community data, audits and structured qualitative work. Where rollout differs between localities, appropriately designed comparisons may be possible.
However, without reliable patient-level exposure and timing, it may be impossible to measure overlap accurately or estimate the effects of particular combinations. An aggregate improvement must not be presented as proof that a particular programme caused it. If neither historical outcomes nor a defensible comparison exist, focus on implementation, reach, equity, patient/carer experience and plausible contribution; use the next service change to establish a prospective evaluation.






TipMatch the Claim to the Evidence





Stronger design: “The analysis estimates a change associated with implementation of the portfolio, subject to the stated assumptions and uncertainty.”
More limited evidence: “The available evidence is consistent with the portfolio contributing to improvement, but the contribution of individual interventions cannot be isolated.”
Do not manufacture precise percentages of contribution where the evidence does not support them.

text:
13. A Practical Portfolio Evidence Summary
Before the commissioning discussion, the team prepares a shared evidence summary rather than five separate and potentially incompatible benefits reports. It also records whether causal impact was estimated, whether only contribution evidence was feasible, and what further evidence is needed for the next decision.

This is not a league table. It makes assumptions, dependencies, costs and evidence visible so that the ICB can discuss maintaining, targeting, combining, redesigning, scaling, further evaluating or disinvesting in services.

Make the Final Decision Conditional on Both Benefit and Safety
The portfolio evidence summary should present benefits, harms and delivery fidelity side by side, rather than relegating them to separate appendices. For each proposed option, commissioners should ask:

Impact: Is there credible evidence of improved outcomes relative to an appropriate comparison, or only descriptive/contribution evidence?
Delivery: Was the intended intervention actually accessible and delivered at sufficient intensity?
Safety and experience: Are there signs of delayed care, adverse outcomes, increased carer burden or poorer experience?
Equity: Are improvements and access distributed fairly relative to underlying need?
Value: What are the incremental costs, opportunity costs and realistic capacity or cash consequences?
Action: Should the ICB maintain, adapt, target, expand, stop or evaluate further — and what evidence would change that choice?

A reasonable conclusion may be continue with targeted redesign and explicit safety monitoring, rather than declaring the whole portfolio either a success or failure. If evidence is weak, document that limitation and make the next change evaluable, using the protocol-design principles in Module 9.


Turn the Discussion into a Testable Commissioning Plan
To complete the example, suppose the ICB decides for illustration only to pilot closer integration between frailty care and UCR in selected localities, while reviewing virtual ward eligibility and the experience of people approaching the end of life. This is an example of how to document a decision, not a conclusion that the evaluation established this option as preferable.
The decision record should state:







Decision component
Illustrative commitment




Reason for change
Test whether accessible care plans and coordinated rapid response improve appropriate care at home


Population and equity
Specify eligibility and monitor uptake across deprivation groups, living arrangements and localities


Resources
Identify the incremental investment, staffing and any double-running costs; do not promise cash savings without a cost-removal plan


Evaluation
Record baseline trends, phased start dates where feasible, patient exposure and an appropriate comparator


Outcomes
Assess appropriate admissions and ED use, patient and carer experience, implementation and unintended effects; separately assess preference-concordant end-of-life care


Implementation fidelity
Monitor eligible-to-treated reach, timeliness, core components delivered, exposure duration and variation between localities


Safety and unintended consequences
Track delayed escalation, readmissions, adverse events, carer burden and any displacement of workload or cost


Reassessment
Agree when to review uptake, implementation, incremental costs, effects and the original assumptions, including what would trigger redesign or discontinuation



The sequence becomes decide → specify expected incremental value → implement and monitor → re-evaluate → revisit the decision. This avoids treating an initial business case or one evaluation as the final word.






TipQuestions for the Commissioning Discussion






Are programmes reaching the same people, and at what points in their pathway?
Are their intended outcomes genuinely the same?
What comparison supports the portfolio’s estimated impact?
Could differences in baseline risk or timing explain apparent programme differences?
Which services are complementary, sequential, substitutive or duplicative?
Have avoided outcomes or monetised benefits been claimed more than once?
What incremental benefits and costs would realistic alternative configurations create?
Who benefits, who might be excluded and what happens to inequalities?
Which benefits release cash, which release capacity and which arise elsewhere?
What remains uncertain, and what additional evidence would change the decision?

title: Module 17: Evaluating Multiple Interventions in Complex Healthcare Systems.qmd
text:
Bringing It All Together
The worked example follows one connected decision pathway:
Shared population and outcomes
↓
Theory of Change and intervention map
↓
Exposure, timing and baseline risk
↓
Credible counterfactual and evaluation design
↓
Interaction and contribution analysis
↓
Quantitative, qualitative and implementation evidence
↓
Reconciled portfolio benefits
↓
STAR-informed comparison of realistic portfolio options
↓
Transparent commissioning judgement and continued learning
The important shift is from “Which programme can claim the improvement?” to:

“What combination of interventions appears to create value for this population, what would change under realistic alternatives, and how confident are we?”
crumbs: 22  Module 17: Evaluating Multiple Interventions in Complex Healthcare Systems.qmd

title: Module 17: Evaluating Multiple Interventions in Complex Healthcare Systems.qmd
text:
Key Takeaways

A reduction in acute activity is not necessarily a net benefit: assess safety, appropriateness, patient and carer experience, equity and unintended consequences alongside utilisation.
Distinguish an intervention that was not delivered as intended from a well-delivered intervention that did not achieve its hypothesised effect; neither distinction alone establishes causality.
An intervention that began without an evaluation plan may still permit retrospective causal analysis; if not, evaluate delivery and contribution without inventing avoided activity, and plan stronger evaluation for the next change.
The patient and population, rather than the programme business case, should help define the evaluation.
Shared outcomes do not mean interventions have identical mechanisms or target exactly the same people.
A fall in admissions is not, on its own, proof of portfolio impact—and is not always the right outcome for end-of-life care.
Exposure, timing, selection bias and the counterfactual are central to credible evaluation.
Interventions can be complementary, sequential, substitutive or duplicative; their benefits should not automatically be added.
Contribution may be more defensible than precise intervention-specific attribution.
Programme claims need reconciliation before estimating portfolio impact or financial value.
STAR-informed resource allocation should compare feasible portfolio alternatives and incremental value, with interactions and uncertainty made explicit.
When linked data are limited, triangulate available evidence and match the strength of the claim to the strength of the design.
Compare incremental costs and benefits against the current portfolio, rather than treating past portfolio impact as the benefit of a new option.
Make equity, contradictory findings, decision assumptions and plans for reassessment explicit.







ImportantThe Question to Remember





Are we evaluating separate services—or understanding what combination of care makes the greatest difference for the people we serve?

text: Who should we intervene with, and why?
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text: 🖨️ Print this module
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
1. Why Population Health Management Matters
Healthcare organisations generate enormous amounts of information about services:

GP appointments
referrals
Emergency Department attendances
hospital admissions
community contacts
waiting lists
procedures
prescribing
outcomes.

These data are essential for understanding how services are being used.
But Population Health Management (PHM) starts with a different question:

What does our population need, and where might a different approach improve outcomes?

This changes the perspective from managing individual services towards understanding populations across organisational and pathway boundaries.
Instead of asking only:

How many emergency admissions did we have?

PHM encourages us to ask:

Which populations are experiencing emergency admissions, how does this relate to their underlying need, what other care are they receiving, where does variation exist, and where might there be an opportunity to intervene differently?







ImportantKey Principle





Population Health Management is not simply about identifying people who use the most healthcare.
It is about understanding population need, variation, inequalities and opportunities for intervention well enough to support better decisions.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

distinguish population need from observed service demand
understand why defining the population and denominator comes before segmentation
recognise what linked patient-level datasets allow us to investigate
understand what linked data cannot tell us on their own
apply PHM principles when linked datasets are unavailable
distinguish segmentation, risk stratification and case finding
distinguish need, utilisation, risk and capacity to benefit
use population intelligence to investigate variation and inequalities
understand the opportunities and limitations of predictive risk
translate population insight into an actionable intervention opportunity
recognise when a question moves from PHM into evaluation.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Level 1 — Population Intelligence
No patient-level linkage is required.
Potential information includes:

demographics
deprivation
disease prevalence
population projections
service activity
outcomes
geographical variation.

The main question is:

Where might need or unexplained variation exist?
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Level 2 — Cohort and Service Intelligence
Some identifiable cohorts or service-level information are available, but linkage across the pathway is incomplete.
Potential information includes:

disease registers
frailty cohorts
service cohorts
referral activity
acceptance rates
service uptake
utilisation profiles
locality comparisons.

The question becomes:

Which populations appear to experience different access, utilisation or outcomes?
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Level 3 — Linked Population Intelligence
Person-level linkage across services enables more detailed longitudinal analysis.
Potential analysis includes:

multimorbidity
longitudinal pathways
service overlap
intervention exposure
sequences of care
outcomes following exposure
more sophisticated segmentation
risk stratification.

The question becomes:

How do people move through the system, which combinations of care do they receive, and what happens subsequently?
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
When the Question Changes
More linked data do not automatically create another level of PHM.
If the question becomes:

Did this intervention cause the improvement?

we have moved into evaluation.
Linked data may make a stronger evaluation possible.
But linkage itself is not an evaluation design.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Looking for Inequalities
Population averages can conceal important differences.
For example, an ICB may show an overall increase in proactive frailty assessment while uptake remains substantially lower in its most deprived neighbourhoods.
PHM can therefore examine variation by relevant characteristics such as:

deprivation
age
geography
ethnicity where data quality permits
care home residence
living circumstances
clinical complexity.

The purpose is not simply to identify differences.
It is to investigate whether those differences reflect:

differing levels of need
access
eligibility
service availability
patient choice
pathway design
data quality
potentially avoidable inequalities.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Scenario A — Population-Level Data
Suppose the ICB has:

population estimates
age profiles
deprivation
estimated frailty prevalence
emergency admission rates
information about community service provision.

The team can compare neighbourhoods and ask:

Where is severe frailty likely to be most prevalent?
Which areas have higher emergency admission rates?
Does variation remain after considering age and population size?
How does community provision vary?
Which areas appear to have high need relative to current service provision?

This can identify areas for further investigation.
It cannot identify individual patients or determine which people received particular services.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
section: Scenario B — Cohort and Service Data
text:
Scenario B — Cohort and Service Data
Suppose the ICB can identify a severe-frailty cohort and has separate information about service activity.
The team can additionally examine:

size of the severe-frailty cohort
referral rates
service uptake
locality differences
changes over time
outcomes at cohort level.

This provides a more focused picture.
But if datasets cannot be linked, the team may still be unable to follow individuals across the entire pathway.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation
text:
Scenario C — Linked Patient-Level Data
Suppose primary care, community and hospital information can be linked at patient level.
The team can now examine:

Person → Frailty → Multimorbidity → Previous utilisation → Intervention exposure → Subsequent pathway → Outcome

This might allow investigation of:

combinations of long-term conditions
previous emergency activity
who receives proactive frailty support
who receives UCR
overlap between services
sequences of care
subsequent emergency activity
variation between patient groups.

This provides a much richer PHM picture.
But an important boundary remains.
Suppose people receiving proactive frailty care subsequently have fewer admissions.
That observation alone still does not establish:

Proactive frailty care caused the reduction.

That is an evaluation question requiring an appropriate counterfactual and evaluation design.






ImportantThe Question Does Not Disappear Because the Data Are Imperfect





The precision of the answer changes.
Use the best available evidence now while improving the information required for the next decision.
crumbs: 23  Module 18: Population Health Management & Population Segmentation

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text: Using scenarios and simulation to explore possible consequences
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
🖨️ Print this module


What might happen if we make this change?
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
1. Why This Module Matters
Healthcare decisions often involve changing systems before we can know exactly what the consequences will be.
An organisation might decide to:

move activity from hospital to community services
introduce a new clinical pathway
expand virtual wards
increase diagnostic capacity
redesign outpatient services
change workforce models
introduce a new triage process
increase preventative activity
consolidate services
respond to expected population growth.

Each decision is based on assumptions about what might happen next.
For example:

If we increase community capacity, emergency admissions will fall.

Or:

If we reduce length of stay, enough hospital capacity will be released to meet future demand.

Or:

If more care moves closer to home, pressure on acute services will reduce.

These may be reasonable hypotheses.
But healthcare systems are complex.
Changing one part of a pathway can affect several others.
A reduction in hospital activity may require substantial additional capacity elsewhere. Removing one bottleneck may simply create another.
Simulation and scenario modelling provide ways of exploring these consequences before changes are fully implemented.






ImportantKey Principle





Simulation is not about predicting the future with certainty.
It is about exploring:

What might happen under different assumptions and different decisions?
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

understand why modelling future scenarios can improve healthcare decisions
distinguish forecasting, scenario analysis, demand and capacity modelling, and simulation
recognise when simple scenario analysis may be sufficient
understand when more sophisticated simulation may add value
recognise how changes in one part of a pathway can affect other services
understand the importance of variability, queues, bottlenecks and resource constraints
interpret simulation outputs without treating them as predictions
challenge the assumptions underlying a model
understand the importance of sensitivity and scenario testing
recognise when modelling complexity is proportionate to the decision being made.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Forecasting
Forecasting typically uses historical patterns to estimate future activity.
For example:

If current trends continue, how many emergency admissions might we expect in three years?

Forecasting can incorporate:

historical trends
population growth
ageing
seasonality
changing prevalence
known service changes.

But forecasting generally assumes that historical relationships provide useful information about the future.
That assumption may become less reliable when the system itself is changing.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Scenario Analysis
Scenario analysis asks:

What happens if we change our assumptions?

For example:

What if referrals increase by 5%?
What if they increase by 15%?
What if workforce capacity falls by 10%?
What if an intervention reduces admissions by 5%, 10% or 15%?
What if the 85+ population grows faster than expected?

These scenarios are not predictions.
They allow decision-makers to explore a range of plausible futures.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Demand and Capacity Modelling
Demand and capacity modelling asks whether the resources available are sufficient to meet expected demand.
For example:

How many appointments are required each week, and how many can the service realistically provide?

This can expose mismatches between:

demand
workforce
appointment capacity
operating hours
bed capacity
diagnostic capacity
treatment capacity.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Simulation
Simulation becomes particularly useful when the system contains:

multiple pathways
queues
variable arrival rates
resource constraints
different patient groups
different service times
interactions between services
uncertainty.

Rather than analysing only averages, simulation can represent how the system behaves over time.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
System Dynamics
System dynamics is useful when the main interest is how parts of a system influence one another over time.
For example:

Workforce shortages → increased workload → burnout → sickness/turnover → further workforce shortages

It focuses more on feedback relationships and system behaviour than individual patient journeys.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them
text:
Monte Carlo Simulation
Monte Carlo methods repeatedly sample uncertain values from specified distributions.
They can help answer questions such as:

Given uncertainty in demand, intervention effect and costs, what range of outcomes might occur?

The purpose is not to identify a single precise future.
It is to represent uncertainty more realistically.
For most decision-makers, knowing which approach is appropriate and why is more important than understanding the technical mathematics behind it.
crumbs: 24  Module 19: Testing Decisions Before We Make Them

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text: Building an evidence spine for better healthcare decisions
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
🖨️ Print this module


How do we combine different forms of evidence into a coherent picture?
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
1. Why This Module Matters
Healthcare decisions are rarely adequately explained by a single dataset, metric or research study.
Decision-makers may know that:

emergency admissions are increasing
referral rates differ between localities
uptake of a service is lower in some population groups
waiting times have increased
outcomes differ between pathways
a new intervention appears to be associated with improvement.

These findings are important. But they often lead to another question:

Why?

Quantitative analysis can identify the scale, distribution and pattern of a problem. It can show how many, how often, where, when, for whom, whether something is changing and whether variation exists.
But numbers alone may not explain why people do not access a service, why clinicians use pathways differently, why an intervention works well in one place but not another, why apparently similar populations experience different outcomes, how patients experience a pathway, what implementation barriers exist, or whether the outcomes being measured are the outcomes that matter most to people.
Qualitative evidence can help answer these questions.






ImportantKey Principle





Quantitative and qualitative evidence are not competing forms of evidence.
They are different ways of understanding the same healthcare system.
Quantitative evidence can help us understand what is happening, how much, where and for whom.
Qualitative evidence can help us understand how, why and under what circumstances it is happening.
Healthcare Decision Intelligence requires both.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

understand why healthcare decisions often require multiple forms of evidence
distinguish quantitative and qualitative evidence without creating an artificial hierarchy between them
recognise different sources of qualitative evidence
understand the role of patient and community insight
understand the role of professional and operational insight
use literature and existing research alongside local evidence
recognise the difference between anecdote and systematically gathered qualitative evidence
understand triangulation
identify agreement, complementarity and disagreement between evidence sources
construct an evidence spine around a healthcare decision
identify important evidence gaps
communicate a balanced evidence picture to decision-makers.

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Patient and Public Experience
Examples include patient interviews, focus groups, listening exercises, patient stories, community conversations, engagement exercises, public consultations, surveys containing free-text responses, complaints, compliments, Patient Advice and Liaison Service information and Healthwatch reports.
These sources can provide insight into barriers to access, experiences of care, communication, continuity, dignity, trust, preferences and outcomes that matter to patients.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Community and Voluntary Sector Insight
Voluntary, community, faith and social enterprise organisations may hold important knowledge about populations that healthcare services do not routinely see.
This might include barriers experienced by particular communities, unmet need, reasons for low service uptake, social circumstances, trust in services, digital exclusion, transport, language and cultural factors.
These organisations may act as trusted intermediaries between communities and statutory organisations. Their existing insight can therefore be an important component of the evidence picture.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Professional and Clinical Insight
Healthcare professionals observe the system from within. Potential sources include clinicians, nurses, pharmacists, allied health professionals, care coordinators, social care professionals and primary care teams.
They may identify pathway problems, inappropriate referrals, gaps between services, duplicated processes, eligibility problems, unintended consequences and changing patient complexity.
Professional opinion should not automatically be treated as fact. But neither should it be dismissed simply because it is not quantitative. It can provide important hypotheses and contextual explanations that can subsequently be tested against other evidence.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Operational Insight
Operational teams often understand practical constraints that are poorly represented in routine datasets. Examples include workforce constraints, referral processes, administrative delays, scheduling problems, capacity constraints, pathway workarounds and data recording practices.
This can be particularly important when quantitative data show unexplained variation.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Formal Qualitative Research
More structured approaches include:

semi-structured interviews
in-depth interviews
focus groups
observation
ethnographic approaches
case studies.

These approaches allow researchers to explore experiences, mechanisms and context systematically.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Existing Engagement Evidence
New engagement should not automatically be the first response to every evidence gap.
Relevant engagement may already have been undertaken by NHS organisations, local authorities, Healthwatch, voluntary organisations, community organisations, universities, charities and service providers.
The first question can therefore be:

What do we already know?

rather than:

Who should we ask again?
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Literature and Existing Research
Qualitative evidence also exists within published research. Literature reviews can identify known barriers to access, patient experiences, implementation challenges, behavioural factors, mechanisms through which interventions may work and evidence from similar populations or settings.
Local qualitative evidence and published research can therefore complement one another.






ImportantExisting Insight Has Value





Do not assume that every decision requires a new engagement exercise.
Start by understanding what patients, communities, professionals and researchers have already told us.
Then identify what remains unknown.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Convergence
Different evidence sources point towards a similar conclusion.
Quantitative evidence: uptake of a service is substantially lower in deprived neighbourhoods.
Qualitative evidence: patients report transport and appointment-time barriers.
Professional insight: staff report difficulty reaching people who cannot attend standard clinic appointments.
Together, these strengthen the hypothesis that access may be contributing to lower uptake.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Complementarity
Different evidence sources tell different parts of the story.
Quantitative evidence: emergency admissions are higher among people living with severe frailty.
Qualitative evidence: patients and carers describe difficulty obtaining support during deterioration outside normal working hours.
The qualitative evidence does not simply confirm the quantitative result. It adds an explanation that was not visible in the numbers.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Disagreement
Evidence sources may conflict.
Routine data: access appears broadly similar between two populations.
But community insight: one population reports substantial difficulty accessing the service.
This should not automatically lead us to discard one source. Instead ask whether we are measuring the right form of access, whether the dataset captures unsuccessful attempts to access care, whether averages conceal subgroup differences, whether the qualitative evidence is drawn from a particular population, whether the service has changed recently, or whether there are data quality problems.






ImportantDisagreement Is Useful Evidence





Triangulation is not about forcing all evidence to agree.
Disagreement can reveal measurement problems, hidden inequalities, different perspectives, missing variables, evidence gaps and incorrect assumptions.
Sometimes the most useful insight comes from asking:

Why don’t these sources agree?

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Step 1 — Establish the Quantitative Picture
Analysis finds that emergency admission rates are higher in several neighbourhoods. These neighbourhoods also have older populations; severe frailty is more prevalent; multimorbidity is higher; deprivation is higher in some areas; and community service utilisation varies substantially.
After adjusting for age and other available measures of need, some variation remains.
This tells decision-makers where the problem appears greatest and which populations are most affected, but it does not fully explain why.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Step 2 — Review Existing Qualitative Evidence
Rather than immediately commissioning new engagement, the Insight team reviews existing sources, including Healthwatch reports, previous patient engagement, voluntary sector intelligence, complaints and free-text feedback, community service reviews, published qualitative research on frailty and existing interviews with carers.
Several themes emerge:

difficulty navigating services
carers being unsure whom to contact during deterioration
concerns about accessing support outside normal hours
poor continuity between services
patients repeating their story to multiple professionals.

These themes provide potential explanations for some of the observed quantitative patterns.
crumbs: 25  Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
section: Step 3 — Gather Professional and Operational Insight
text:
Step 3 — Gather Professional and Operational Insight
Discussions with professionals identify additional issues:

variation in referral thresholds
differences in awareness of community alternatives
inconsistent availability of rapid response services
workforce constraints
variation in how frailty is recorded.

This generates hypotheses that can be checked against available data. For example:

Do areas with lower UCR utilisation have higher emergency admission rates after accounting for population need?

The qualitative evidence has therefore generated a testable analytical question.

title: Module 20: Bringing Evidence Together
text:
Step 5 — Construct the Evidence Spine

Population need
Older population + frailty + multimorbidity
↓
Observed pattern
Higher emergency admissions in some neighbourhoods
↓
Unexplained variation
Population need explains some, but not all, of the difference
↓
Qualitative insight
Patients and carers describe difficulties accessing timely support
↓
Professional and operational insight
Referral practices and community capacity vary
↓
External evidence
Timely community responses may support some people safely at home
↓
Intervention hypothesis
More consistent access to proactive and urgent community support may reduce avoidable escalation for some people with frailty
↓
Decision
Consider whether targeted pathway redesign should be developed and evaluated.

Notice what the evidence spine does not say:

Community services will definitely reduce emergency admissions.

The evidence supports a plausible intervention hypothesis. It does not remove uncertainty.

title: Module 21: From Evidence to Decision
section: 1. Why Evidence Does Not Make the Decision
text:
1. Why Evidence Does Not Make the Decision
Throughout this series we have explored how healthcare decision-makers can make better use of:

data
statistical analysis
evaluation
health economics
population health intelligence
scenario modelling
qualitative evidence
research
professional expertise
lived experience.

But even excellent evidence does not automatically tell us what to do.
Imagine an intervention where the evidence suggests that it:

improves patient outcomes
is valued by patients
could reduce pressure elsewhere in the system
appears economically attractive.

There may still be difficult questions.
Can we afford it?
Do we have the workforce?
What would we have to stop doing to fund it?
Who would benefit?
Could some populations benefit more than others?
Could it widen inequalities?
How certain are we about the expected benefits?
Is there a better alternative?
These questions require judgement.






ImportantKey Principle





The purpose of Healthcare Decision Intelligence is not to remove judgement from healthcare decisions.
It is to make that judgement:

better informed
more explicit
more transparent
more consistent
more defensible.

title: Module 21: From Evidence to Decision
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you should be able to:

distinguish evidence generation from decision-making
define the decision before considering solutions
use an evidence spine to support a decision
identify realistic alternative options
make decision criteria explicit
recognise and communicate trade-offs
consider equity alongside effectiveness and value
incorporate uncertainty into the decision
understand the role of deliberation and judgement
document the rationale for a decision
specify what should be monitored and evaluated afterwards
recognise when a decision should be reconsidered.

title: Module 21: From Evidence to Decision
text:
The Evidence Spine

Population Need
Population analysis shows:

growth in older age groups
increasing frailty
increasing multimorbidity
geographical variation in need.



Quantitative Evidence
Analysis shows:

high emergency admission rates among people with severe frailty
substantial variation between localities
variation in community service utilisation.



Qualitative Evidence
Patients and carers describe:

difficulty navigating services
uncertainty about whom to contact during deterioration
problems obtaining timely support
poor continuity between services.



Professional and Operational Evidence
Teams identify:

variation in referral practices
workforce constraints
inconsistent community capacity
differences in pathway availability.



Evaluation Evidence
Available evidence suggests proactive and rapid community interventions may contribute to improved outcomes and reduced escalation for some patients.
However, precise attribution remains uncertain.


Health Economics
Expansion requires additional investment.
Potential benefits include:

improved outcomes
improved patient experience
hospital capacity released
potentially avoided future costs.

Not all benefits represent cash-releasing savings.


Scenario Modelling
Modelling suggests that shifting activity upstream is feasible only if sufficient community capacity is available.
Without that capacity, the bottleneck may simply move from hospital to community services.

title: Module 21: From Evidence to Decision
text:
The Decision
After considering the evidence, resources, equity, feasibility and uncertainty, the ICB might decide:

Proceed with phased expansion targeted initially towards populations with the greatest need, accompanied by prospective evaluation and agreed review points.

The important point is not whether this hypothetical decision is “correct”.
It is that the rationale is visible.
Decision-makers can explain:

what problem they were addressing
what evidence they considered
which alternatives were available
which trade-offs they accepted
what remained uncertain
why the selected option was preferred.

That is a more defensible decision.
